clue.text: Result of killing a gazelle, perhaps?

definitions.text: Result of killing a gazelle, perhaps?

parts.words: Result of killing a gazelle, perhaps?
parts.note: a gazelle is a swift male antelope of sorts, so bagging one yields a quick male deer; the idiom means money made easily and quickly

explanation.surface: A hunter wonders what comes of shooting a gazelle.
explanation.walkthrough: A buck is a male antelope and also slang for a dollar; a gazelle is famously fast, hence the pun on easy money.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for money earned quickly and with little effort, often dubiously.

clue.text: Carry out raids over a long period

parts.note: over a period means for that period
an age is a long period

explanation.surface: Conducting raids across a long stretch of time.
explanation.definitionFit: To raid or ravage in search of supplies, the old military sense of the verb.

clue.text: County now divided, by sea

parts.note: a coastal English county on the Channel, split into East and West halves

explanation.surface: A seaside county has been split in two.
explanation.walkthrough: SUSSEX is a county on England's south coast, divided administratively into East and West Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: A historic county on the English Channel, now split into two administrative areas.

clue.text: Like any question, not altogether right?

definitions.text: Like any question, not altogether right?

parts.words: Like any question, not altogether right?
parts.note: every question has two sides, so it is not all right side but also left side

explanation.surface: Any question is a little bit wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not altogether right' sounds like 'slightly wrong' but means having a left side as well as a right one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means having two sides, as every question is said to.

clue.text: Sort of radio Gilpin was in charge of

definitions.meaning: short-range two-way radio used by truckers
Cowper's John Gilpin was 'a citizen of credit and renown' and 'a train-band captain'

explanation.surface: A kind of radio once run by a man named Gilpin.
explanation.walkthrough: William Cowper's comic poem John Gilpin describes him as a London citizen and captain of a train-band, so a citizen's band.
explanation.definitionFit: A short-range radio service for private users; read literally, a band led by a townsman.

clue.text: Vessel kept going by a couple of banks

definitions.text: Vessel kept going by a couple of banks

parts.words: Vessel kept going by a couple of banks
parts.note: the banks are tiers of oars, not financial institutions; an ancient galley rowed with two such tiers

explanation.surface: A ship or business propped up financially by two lenders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' suggests lenders funding an enterprise; here it means rows of oarsmen, one above the other.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient galley with two tiers of oars on each side, the bi- prefix meaning two.

clue.text: Britons taking diamonds to part of Ireland

parts.note: ice is slang for diamonds
NI is Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Ancient Britons carry gems over to Ulster.
explanation.walkthrough: The ICENI were the ancient British tribe led by Boudicca.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient tribe of eastern England, so a people of early Britain.

clue.text: Get us oil, as ordered, for puffer

indicators.note: the letters are put into a fresh order, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone asks for oil to be fetched for a smoker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as ordered' rearranges GET US OIL. A 'puffer' here is one who puffs, or praises lavishly.
explanation.definitionFit: To puff is to praise extravagantly, so a puffer is one who delivers glowing tributes.

clue.text: There's no difficulty in getting freedom from pain

definitions.meaning: the quality of being simple to do

explanation.surface: Being pain-free comes without trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means simplicity of a task, and also comfort, being relieved of discomfort.

clue.text: Firm made to form Trade Union -or else

indicators.note: the letters are forced into a new shape, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A company is forced to create a union for its workers, under threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made to form' rearranges TU plus OR ELSE into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone determined and unwavering, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Demand of interrogators for name of divine female

definitions.meaning: questioners insist that a suspect speak to them
the Roman goddess of the earth

explanation.surface: Questioners demand the name of a goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is an order to speak; as one, it names the Roman earth goddess.

clue.text: March onto Cook's vessel, a merchant ship

parts.note: to march heavily is to tramp
a steamer is a cook's pan for steaming food, not Captain Cook's ship

explanation.surface: Someone marches aboard Captain Cook's ship, a trader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook's vessel' suggests Captain Cook's Endeavour; it is a kitchen pan.
explanation.definitionFit: A cargo ship with no fixed route, taking freight wherever it is offered.

clue.text: County's gifted opener departed

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', linking definition to wordplay

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, here of gifted

parts.note: departed means went, left

explanation.surface: A talented opening batsman from the county has left.
explanation.walkthrough: GWENT is a former county in south-east Wales. 'opener' suggests cricket but simply takes the first letter of 'gifted'.
explanation.definitionFit: A historic Welsh county, an example of the class named.

clue.text: Focusing on emptiness of trap?

parts.note: emptiness means nothing, zero
read as 'contained in', so the zero sits in the trap
a gin is a snare or trap for animals

explanation.surface: Concentrating on how empty a snare is.
explanation.walkthrough: Read cryptically, 'emptiness of trap' is nought in a gin, the old word for a snare.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means narrowing attention or aim on a target.

clue.text: Painter making relative profit, so to speak

parts.note: a grandma is a relative
profit spoken sounds like prophet, and Moses is the archetypal prophet

explanation.surface: An artist making money out of a family member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so to speak' turns 'profit' into its sound-alike 'prophet', of whom Moses is the example. The painter was the American folk artist who began painting in old age.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Mary Robertson, a celebrated American primitive artist, worked under this nickname.

clue.text: "La mer" most turbulent here

indicators.note: turbulent water churns, so the letters are churned up

explanation.surface: The sea is at its stormiest in this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turbulent' rearranges LA MER and MOST; the whole clue describes a whirlpool.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent whirlpool, where the sea is wildest.

clue.text: One act delayed for devoted fan

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
to act is to do
delayed means later

explanation.surface: A single performance is postponed for an ardent admirer.
explanation.definitionFit: A worshipper of an idol, so an adoring follower.

clue.text: Acts cancelled, so stops broadcast

parts.note: music-hall acts are turns
a cancelled event is off

explanation.surface: Performances are axed, so transmission ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Switching off a radio or television ends the transmission you receive.

clue.text: Instruments to amplify sound from headquarters

parts.note: to amplify is to increase, to double

indicators.note: the clue asks for a word heard like the one the next word gives

parts.note: headquarters are bases

explanation.surface: Equipment for boosting the audio coming from central command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound from' makes BASES heard as BASSES. 'sound' looks like the thing amplified but is the homophone signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest bowed string instruments of the orchestra, examples of the class named.

clue.text: Feline, long ago on board

indicators.note: being on board a vessel means inside it, so one piece goes inside the vessel

parts.note: board suggests the vessel boarded, a boat
BC, before Christ, dates from long ago

explanation.surface: A cat from ancient times on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' means inside a boat: BC goes into BOAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild North American lynx, an example of the cat family.

clue.text: Lack of this batsman leaving a lot unsettled?

definitions.text: Lack of this batsman leaving a lot unsettled?

parts.words: Lack of this batsman leaving a lot unsettled?
parts.note: without a tin-opening tool, lots of cans stay closed; also a first-in cricketer

explanation.surface: Missing a first batsman leaves the team rattled.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both a cricketer who bats first and a tool for opening tins; 'unsettled' hints at unopened.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman who starts the innings, and also a gadget for opening tins.

clue.text: Sort of weather forecast for Rockies, perhaps

definitions.meaning: the Rocky Mountains are an extended chain of mountains

explanation.surface: A kind of weather outlook for the Rocky Mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a forecast covering a distant period, and read literally a lengthy mountain chain.

clue.text: Where boats anchor in island sound

indicators.note: the word given is spoken, and its sound-alike is entered

parts.note: Rhodes is a Greek island

explanation.surface: Boats moor in a strait by an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like a strait of water but is the homophone signal: RHODES heard as ROADS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheltered water off shore where ships ride at anchor, also called a roadstead.

clue.text: Novel device for lifting

definitions.meaning: something novel is new, like an exclusive news story
a shovel-like tool for lifting loose material or ice cream

explanation.surface: An inventive gadget for hoisting things.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's exclusive story is something new; the same word names a ladle-like implement.

clue.text: Hard worker a victim of long-term investment

definitions.meaning: investment here means siege; the citizens of Troy suffered a ten-year siege

explanation.surface: A diligent employee loses out on a long-term financial plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'investment' is the old military sense: besieging a town. Troy was besieged for ten years.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who toils tirelessly, from an idiom; also a citizen of Troy, besieged for a decade.

clue.text: In Paris for the music, good and dead as Wilde said

definitions.text: In Paris for the music, good and dead as Wilde said

parts.words: In Paris for the music, good and dead as Wilde said
parts.note: Gershwin wrote a tone poem about a US visitor in Paris, and Wilde quipped that good US citizens go to Paris when they die

explanation.surface: Someone visits Paris for the music, recalling a Wilde epigram about the dead.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde wrote 'Good Americans, when they die, go to Paris'; Gershwin's piece is 'An American in Paris'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from the United States, the figure both the Gershwin title and the Wilde quip describe.

clue.text: Jib at clearing rubbish

definitions.meaning: to jib at something is to balk at or decline it

explanation.surface: Someone balks at clearing away the garbage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clearing' only links the two senses, adding the picture of bin collection.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means decline or balk; as a noun, stressed on the first syllable, it means waste.

clue.text: Linesman helping the poor players?

parts.note: not a football official but someone in the wings who feeds actors their forgotten lines

explanation.surface: A football official helps a weak team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linesman' and 'players' suggest sport; the players are actors, as in Macbeth's 'poor player'.
explanation.definitionFit: The theatre worker who supplies actors with forgotten lines during a performance.
